description: We are Aspirants of SpaceX, a team of curious and motivated students passionate about space exploration, technology, software development, AI, and innovation. We love learning new technologies and turning creative ideas into meaningful projects.
summary:
We built "Abandoned, But Not Forgotten", a pixel-art storytelling website for school-age space fans. The guide is "Elias 2-24 b", a young planet who has never heard of human spacecraft. 

The journey has 17 discoveries across the Moon, Mars and deep space, plus an opening scene and two bonus lessons. Each stop has Elias's dialogue, a fact card and a scrapbook entry. 

Interactive elements include a moonquake seismograph, a laser-aiming game, driving games, a helicopter take-off and hover game, a lander, a flashlight search, ordering puzzles and a quiz. A Space Scrapbook fills up as Elias learns, and Elias can read the story aloud using the browser's built-in voice.

The challenge is to tell the story of NASA's left-behind hardware on the Moon and Mars to school-age space enthusiasts. 
our project answers 3 critical questions-

- What was left behind?
- Why it was left?
- Why it still matters?


Left-behind spacecraft can look like debris, but they are evidence of what humans learned, from measuring the Earth–Moon distance with a laser mirror to hearing moonquakes. As more missions head to the Moon and Mars, young people also need to understand why the historic sites must be protected from future explorers. By making that history interactive, we help students connect with real NASA missions, build curiosity about science and engineering, and think about what humanity chooses to leave behind next.
details:
We a created a free, browser-based, pixel-art storytelling adventure for school-age space fans. It tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars.

The user follows Elias 2-24 b, a baby planet who has never heard of human spacecraft. His scanner finds objects marked “ORIGIN: EARTH” on other worlds, and the user learns alongside him. The journey has 20 screens:

an opening scene,

17 discoveries across the Moon, Mars and deep space,

2 bonus lessons, “The Weight Problem” and “Protect the Footprint”.

It explores the following places and discoveries

Moon - Surveyor landers, Apollo descent stage, ALSEP seismometers, laser retroreflector, Lunar Roving Vehicles, personal objects (family photo, golf balls, flags)

Mars - Viking, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, landing hardware, impact debris

Deep space - Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler

Each stop includes Elias’s dialogue, a fact card, a scrapbook entry and usually a mini-game. The site also has a Space Scrapbook that fills up, a Back button, and optional spoken narration.

Technical design.

The whole site is in an index.html file. The story is stored as a list of scenes (title, dialogue, fact, scrapbook line, game), and a small engine plays them one by one.

Each game is a function that tells the engine when the player has won.

Games with movement use the HTML canvas. Others use ordinary page elements.

A skip button appears after 20 seconds so nobody gets stuck.

Narration uses the browser’s built-in text-to-speech, with a settings panel to change voice, pitch and speed.

Elias’s picture is built into the file, so the site needs no database, server code or accounts.

Benefits

Engaging for children. The story, humor and games make real mission history feel like play, not a database of facts.

It's Accessible, It’s free, needs no install, and runs on a laptop or phone.

A clear message is conveyed . It changes “space junk” into “history and science”, with each object shown as “once a scientist”.

Responsible exploration

Young users learn why historic sites on the Moon need protecting from future explorers.

Low-cost and easy to update.

One file makes it simple to host and to edit.

We hope to help students connect with real NASA missions and the science each one made possible.

Spark curiosity about science, engineering and space exploration.

Build awareness that exploration leaves footprints, and that people must choose responsibly what to leave behind.

Grow the project into a classroom resource, with more missions (such as later Mars missions and Chinese or Indian lunar missions), translations, a more child-like narrator voice and teacher worksheets.

Tools, languages and software used

Languages- HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or libraries)

Graphics - HTML canvas for games, CSS for the Moon and Mars terrain, emoji for objects, the Press Start 2P pixel font (Google Fonts), and the Elias mascot art got using ai inspired from NASA's blog.

Audio-The browser’s Web Speech API for narration

Hosting -netlify


Our Project is creative in the following ways
1. A new point of view: We tell the story through Elias 2-24 b, a baby planet who knows nothing about humans. The user discovers the objects with him, so the learning feels like curiosity, not a lecture.

2. Changing “space junk” into history: The challenge could be read as a story about waste. We turned it around: “Every machine here was once a scientist.” The finale crosses out “SPACE JUNK”, then “LEFT-BEHIND OBJECTS”, and replaces them with “MISSION FOOTPRINTS”. The same idea carries through the slogan “Abandoned does not mean useless.”

3. Games that teach the science: Each game is tied to what the object actually did.

4. A retro pixel-art style with a personal touch: The pixel look suits school-age users and the “old hardware” theme. The Space Scrapbook gives children something to collect, and Elias can read the story aloud.

5. Humor and emotion together: Moon golf balls and “a really long parking break” for the rovers make children smile. Charles Duke’s family photo and the idea of protecting footprints add a more thoughtful moment.

Factors Considered

Audience: School-age children, so short lines, simple words, a friendly character and a non-graphic treatment of the astronaut waste items (“personal consumables”).

Preservation: Using NASA’s lunar heritage recommendations (contact, dust, exhaust, contamination) so the project also explains why these sites must be protected.

Chronology: Moving from the Moon to Mars to deep space, so the story shows how exploration advanced.

Accessibility: One free web page, no install or account, keyboard, mouse and touch controls, a skip button if a game is too hard, and an option to turn the voice off.
